verdict.reasoning: The patient reports: "I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment. I got stung by a wasp recently" indicating difficulty breathing after the sting.
The patient says: "I got stung by a wasp recently. Well, I'm not sure whether it's kind of bitten or stung... one of the two... a B and a wasp. But one of the two? Yeah, it was one of the two."
The patient states: "I'm feeling like slightly anxious" in the context of describing the sting and breathing difficulty.
The patient reports: "I've got a bit of a rash on my arm where I got stung" and later confirms rash on the arm.
Repeated from cc-001: "I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment. I got stung by a wasp recently" clearly links difficulty breathing to the sting.
The patient says: "potentially there's a bit of swelling in my lips and tongue. Feels a bit weird."
In response to anxiety questions: Patient: "Yeah, sometimes. Occasionally."
The patient states: "I've had eczema before. That's kind of the major thing."
Allergy history: Patient: "I'm allergic to penicillin."
Social history: Patient: "I am a computer scientist."
Living situation: Patient: "Yes" when asked "And you're living alone?"
Pets: Patient: "I have a cat."
Exam description: Doctor: "It's slightly red, yeah. And kind of there's a bit of a. Like a hole where..." Patient (clinician) clarifies: "Yes. Yeah. The puncture mark."

The clinician notes: "Your breathing seems all right to me right now" and later: "based on... how you're breathing... I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction" indicating normal-appearing breathing on exam.
The clinician says: "your, your lips don't seem swollen to me right now" and later: "you mentioned swelling of your lip. Thankfully, I can't see any of that right now."
Assessment: "It seems to me that this is a localized allergic reaction" and repeatedly refers to it as reaction to an insect bite/sting.

History and exam: rash and slight local reaction described: "I've got a bit of a rash on my arm"; exam shows slight redness. Breathing: patient says difficulty but "I don't feel like it's like particularly acute" and clinician says breathing seems all right. This matches rash/slight swelling plus mild, not acutely severe breathing difficulty after the sting.
Plan: "you can get pyritone or chlorphenamine and you can take one tablet, four milligrams, up to about six times a day."

Plan: "If the redness in your arm spreads and it feels hot or, you know, you have signs of any localised infection, we may need to think about other treatments..." This is monitoring for spreading redness or local infection.

The clinician educates on urgent signs: "what those signs and symptoms are... swelling of the lips, difficulty breathing, you might have something called stridor..." and advises going to A&E if these occur.
Plan: "I'm going to leave some information about anaphylactic reactions just for you to read about it."

Follow-up advice: "if anything changes, if anything deteriorates, either make an appointment with us or go straight to ae" and "if it was to happen that... on a regular basis... you might need to think about blood testing" plus "Get back to us if you're feeling worried."
